subject: strandbeest
pitch:
Category: Abstract.
Subject: wind-walking beach creature of tubes.
Style: Theo Jansen kinetic sculpture.
reasoning:
I'm planning a Strandbeest-like creature with PVC-pipe tubes, Jansen linkage legs, and sail-like wings standing on a beach, roughly 3m long and 2m tall, facing forward with a yellow tubular central frame.

Since this is a static model, I'll skip rigging detailed joints and instead rely on plain rod and part objects without bones, keeping things simple. For the legs, I'm working through the classic Jansen linkage math—standard link lengths and crank geometry—to compute each leg segment's position via circle intersections at different crank phases across several leg units per side.

Still working out the linkage topology... K as the intersection of circles centered at A (radius b) and P (radius j), then L as the intersection of circles centered at A (radius c) and K (radius d), continuing to trace each joint through the chain.

I'm working through the joint definitions for this linkage mechanism, trying to piece together which points connect to form the triangle K-L-M, then figuring out how the ankle joint N and foot point O attach using the remaining intersection distances.

Since I can't actually run the computation to verify intersections, I need to guard against bad geometry: if a circle-circle intersection fails, I'll fall back to something reasonable like a midpoint. I also need to normalize the whole cycle so the foot's lowest point touches the floor, and pick the correct intersection side (upper vs lower) so the leg hangs below the hip in a sensible orientation.

I'll just pick consistent sides for each joint pragmatically, and if the foot ends up above the body I'll mirror the y-values to fix orientation; if a joint has no valid intersection, I'll clamp to the nearest feasible point along the line rather than fail. The exact linkage geometry matters less than the overall visual, so I'll scale the ~65-unit leg height down to roughly 0.78 meters for the final sculpture.

Rethinking the scale, I want the leg span closer to 1.3m with an overall sculpture height around 2.6m including sails. For layout, I'm simplifying the real Strandbeest's 13-paired crankshaft into a single crank axle along X, placing leg units at various z positions with inner and outer leg pairs offset in x, and now I'm working out where each unit's crank center sits relative to that axle.

Settling on a simplified structure: 6 units spaced along z, each with 2 sides and phase offsets of 60° per unit plus 180° between sides, giving 6 short axle rods instead of a full 13-crank arrangement.

I'm also adding supporting structure—longitudinal top beam tubes connecting the A points along the frame, plus vertical truss frames at each unit—and offsetting each leg's crank-side links slightly in x to avoid visual overlap between parts.

Mapping out the full linkage for each leg: roughly 11 rods and 8 pin joints per leg, with yellow tube links, small dark pin spheres at nodes, and a rubber foot capsule at the ground contact point.

Across twelve legs that totals around 240 parts, safely under budget, with hexagonal-sided rods for simplicity. For resting pose, I want to find the global minimum foot height across all legs given their phase offsets, then set hip height so the lowest foot touches the floor with the correct foot radius.

Now I'm working out the 2D leg coordinate frame with u along the forward direction and v as height, picking a consistent orientation so both sides walk the same way. With the scale factor giving roughly 0.76m crank length and 1.2m leg width, I need to offset each unit along x since six units spaced 0.6m apart would otherwise overlap and collide visually if placed in the same plane.

Each unit's x-offset will fan out progressively (roughly 0.28 to 0.58m across the six units plus a small crank-side offset), giving the body a tapered, layered look about 1.3m wide, with the axle for each unit spanning symmetrically across its own x-offset. I'm also planning to connect the A-points on each side with a stepped tube-like beam running as a polyline through them, plus vertical struts tying them up to the top frame.

Now I'm fleshing out the top structure: twin longitudinal beams running along the top, cross beams at each unit's z-position, and diagonal braces connecting the top frame down to each A-point. For aesthetic flair I'm adding Jansen-style wind-catching elements — a rear sail frame with fabric panels and a mast with shroud lines, a rounded nose hoop at the front, and rows of bottle-like capsule shapes mounted along the top beams to evoke a "stomach" of bottles.

I'm settling on the color palette: yellow tubes, black pins, white zip-ties, pale translucent blue for bottles and caps, and tan sail cloth. I'm deciding to skip adding a sand floor or footprints to keep things simple, and working out how to position the foot spheres so the lowest points just touch or barely sink into the ground plane.

Now I'm computing the overall leg height and scale factor, checking that the Jansen linkage proportions translate to a reasonable strandbeest height of roughly 1.5-2 meters without making the legs too tall.

I'm defining a circle-intersection helper that finds where two circles meet, then working out a chirality heuristic to pick the correct intersection sign for each joint point.

Working through the intersection math for K, I get two candidate positions and need to figure out which matches the actual linkage geometry — then I continue chaining through L and M using similar circle-intersection calculations, though I'm uncertain whether I'm placing the joints correctly relative to the picture I remember.

Computing M from K and L gives roughly (-14.7,-72.7), which looks like a plausible foot position down near -73, so this might actually be the foot joint itself. I'll treat M as the foot candidate from this two-bar sub-leg and move on to figuring out the remaining joints.

Still working out the linkage geometry...

Working out the axle and crank arm geometry for each leg unit, spacing the A-positions along z from about -1.4 to 1.35, and figuring how the crank pin P connects via a rod offset from the axle at C to attach the linkage arms.

Still working out link plane positions...

Let me simplify the frame geometry instead: cross beams at each x_i level connecting to longitudinal rails at fixed x positions, with top beams and verticals linking them into a proper truss structure.

For the sails, I'll go with a large wing-like main sail mounted on a mast toward the rear, plus rows of smaller bottle-style sails along the top rail, and an arched bow structure at the front for visual interest.

I'm placing a main sail behind the mast and a smaller jib in front, giving them thin extruded cloth panels with batten ribs and a dark orange stripe. Then I'm designing the signature "bottle wings" -- rows of vertical pale plastic bottle shapes with blue caps mounted along the top beams on both sides, mimicking Theo Jansen's paddle-like vanes.

I'm adding small white torus rings at beam joints to mimic zip ties, dark cylindrical end caps on the yellow tubes, and alternating two shades of yellow across units to give the legs some visual depth and variation.

Now I'm figuring out foot-sink and leg phasing—setting each leg's crank phase offset using a 137° rotation plus a 180° flip for the mirrored side, computing the crank position from the center using cosine/sine of that angle, and determining the lowest foot point across all legs to establish ground contact.

I'm writing position and rod helper functions: a coordinate mapper that places each leg joint in world space scaled by a factor and offset so the lowest foot touches the ground, and a rod-drawing helper for connecting joints with cylindrical links, flat-capped for a clean tube look at the pins.

Now I'm deciding against using bones/joints for articulation, opting for a fully static rest-pose model since the creature's abstract shape doesn't require animation rigging. For the bottles, I'm planning to build them from a cylindrical body plus a tapered shoulder and cap, oriented vertically.

Actually, I realize a single lathe operation could capture the whole bottle profile—body, shoulder taper, and neck—in one swept outline, with a separate cap cylinder added on top. I'll keep it simple without glow effects, and consider tilting the bottles slightly outward for visual variety.

I'm also thinking about adding small abstract details to give the creature more character—maybe a front-mounted wind-vane arm with a small triangular flag to act like a feeler or sensor, since these beasts have no real head to speak of.

Now I'm setting up the color palette (yellows, cloth tones, bottle blues, rope browns) and defining the core Jansen linkage geometry function that computes each leg joint position from the driving angle.

Setting up unit spacing and building cross beams, axles, and connecting rods...

Still defining leg geometry...

Setting foot radius at 0.035 and sketching the frame geometry: long bottom/top beams, verticals at each z-position, alternating diagonals forming a Warren truss, plus top cross beams and wider outer rails for bottle placement.

For the bows, I'm defining a front hoop using a catmull-rom sweep through curved points rising over the frame, with a similar taller rear arch for the mast stay, and locating the mast base at the center of the top cross beam.

Now I'm adding mast stays as thin rope-like rods connecting the mast top to the hoops, then shaping the main sail as an extruded outline running behind the mast using swept coordinate points.

Now I'm sketching the jib as a forward triangle running from mast to forestay, giving it an orange cloth material distinct from the main sail's striped panel overlay. I'm also adding a decorative emblem on the sail—a ring with spoke rods made from a torus and thin cylinders, mirrored on both sides of the sail surface.

For the deck, I'm placing rows of bottle sails along the outer rails on each side, spaced along the z-axis with alternating cap colors, then checking the overall height math so the mast and sail still clear the bottle tops comfortably.

I'm adding small white tori as zip-tie rings at the beam joints, taking advantage of the default torus orientation lining up naturally with the longitudinal beams, and considering whether to cap the cross-beam ends with dark cylinder plugs.

I should add a wind vane up front with a small arm and arrow fin, plus a pair of shroud lines running from the mast top down to rail points for extra rigging detail. Time to write the actual code now.

For the bottle, I'm lathing a tilted outline with a tapered neck and cap, normalizing the tilt axis, then adding a small cylinder cap on top and extruding the label with proper thickness and color.

Now I'm working out the extrude orientation so thickness aligns correctly, then figuring out where to place a torus emblem on the sail, making sure its axis points sideways rather than the default.

I'm checking that the emblem position and radius keep it fully within the sail's triangular outline, then sketching coordinates for an orange stripe band near the sail's bottom edge.

Now I'm computing the three emblem spokes radiating from center to ring, mapping sail-local coordinates into world space via helper functions for z and y, before setting up intersection-picking logic.

Writing circle intersection function...

Now I'm thinking through the axle mounting — since the axle floats independently, I should add a diagonal strut connecting the axle's center to the cross beam, plus a small bearing block at that junction to visually anchor it. Then I'll finalize the module code.
